first_impression.reaction: Typed 'same sex marriage greece' on the train because my partner and I keep saying 'Greece, one day'. The first word is 'Yes.' with a date and the date the law changed. That's exactly what I wanted. I'd read the takeaways, the bit on foreigners and the LGBT friendly section, glance at the FAQ, then bookmark it.

journey.quote: Yes. As at November 2026, same-sex marriage in Greece is legal: Greek law allows a civil marriage between two persons of different or the same sex, and the change has been in force since 16 February 2024.
journey.reaction: First word answers my question, and it's dated this month. That's the 'is this still true?' worry gone straight away.

journey.quote: For an Australian couple, the questions are practical.
journey.reaction: Ah, it's written for Australians. We're in Singapore. The legal bit still works for me, but I can tell some of the paperwork won't.

journey.quote: The law does not address foreign nationals, so the municipality where you marry sets the paperwork, and Rhodes, for one, asks for a certificate of no impediment naming your partner, translated into Greek and apostilled.
journey.reaction: Useful, but it's a long one to read on a phone. I had to go over it twice to get that 'the island decides the paperwork' is the main point.

journey.section: Is same-sex marriage legal in Greece?
journey.quote: Article 1350 now reads: "Marriage is contracted between two persons of different or the same sex. Marriage requires the agreement of the intending spouses."
journey.reaction: The actual wording of the law, plus a link to the official text. That's proper, not a blog guessing.

journey.section: Can foreigners have a same-sex wedding in Greece?
journey.quote: The short answer is that the civil route is the one open to you, and it runs through the municipality where you marry.
journey.reaction: Heading matches my next question and there's a short answer up top. Good.

journey.quote: So the question to put to the municipality is direct: what do two Australian citizens, neither of them resident in Greece, need to give you, and by when?
journey.reaction: So do I need to live there or not? The honest answer seems to be 'the law doesn't say, ask the town'. Fair, but I'd hoped for a clearer yes or no.

journey.quote: Every notarial service needs an appointment, Monday to Friday, 9:00am to 12:30pm, though apostille and CNI documents can be submitted by post.
journey.reaction: Embassy opening hours. Very thorough for Australians, but for me this is the part I scroll past.

journey.section: Is Greece LGBT friendly for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Avoid public displays of affection, especially in rural areas. Attitudes are generally more accepting on Greek islands such as Mykonos, Santorini and Ios.
journey.reaction: Honestly this is what I actually worry about. They didn't sugar-coat it and they quoted a government source. I trust the page more for it.

journey.section: Is Greece LGBT friendly for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Racially motivated and homophobic attacks have occurred.
journey.reaction: Bit of a gut punch to read, but I'd rather know. It doesn't put me off Greece, it just tells me which islands to look at.

journey.quote: In Lindos, the municipality lists St Paul's chapel platform, a tiny chapel below a cliff in the shadow of the Acropolis of Lindos, beside the turquoise water of St Paul's Bay.
journey.reaction: Okay, now I'm picturing it. A legal ceremony there, by the sea? Screenshot for my partner.

journey.quote: Have you hosted same-sex weddings before, and will you put that in writing?
journey.reaction: This is the question I'd be nervous to ask, and the page just tells me to ask it. Good list, easy to scan.

journey.section: Legal ceremony, symbolic celebration or both
journey.quote: There are three ways to shape the day, and each suits a different couple.
journey.reaction: Three bold options, short paragraphs. Makes it clear we could marry legally at home and just party in Greece.

journey.section: Same-sex marriage in Greece questions, answered
journey.quote: Can we have a symbolic same-sex wedding in Santorini or Mykonos?
journey.reaction: FAQ answers mostly repeat what I read above, which is fine for skimmers. This last one was new and answered in one line.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around your civil ceremony, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins
journey.reaction: Quotes in AUD. So this is an Australian business. Not sure they'd work with a Singapore couple.

unanswered_questions: Does a couple living outside Australia, for example in Singapore, follow the same CNI route, or do we go to our own embassy in Athens?
Is there any island where it's known that the registrar has already married same-sex couples, so we're not the first?
Do you work with couples who aren't Australian?

turn_offs_found.quote: The law does not address foreign nationals, so the municipality where you marry sets the paperwork, and Rhodes, for one, asks for a certificate of no impediment naming your partner, translated into Greek and apostilled.
turn_offs_found.why: Takeaways are what I read first on the phone, and this one packs three ideas into one sentence. The main point, that the island's municipality decides your paperwork, gets lost behind the Rhodes detail.

turn_offs_found.quote: For an Australian couple, the questions are practical.
turn_offs_found.why: It narrows the page to Australians in the second paragraph. The legal answer applies to anyone, so a non-Australian searcher starts wondering what else won't apply to them.

would_share_with: My partner, for the 'Yes' answer and the Lindos chapel line
A friend who keeps asking if Greece is safe for gay couples, for the Smartraveller section

cta_reaction.why: I came to find out if it's legal, not to book anything, and we're nowhere near planning. No pop-ups, so the links didn't annoy me, but 'quotes in AUD' makes me think I'm not who they're for. I'd bookmark the page.

top_3_changes: Split the second Key takeaway so the first sentence says only that the municipality where you marry sets the paperwork, with the Rhodes example as a short follow-on, so it reads in one pass on a phone.
In 'What Australians arrange' or the foreigners section, add one line for non-Australian couples (check your own embassy's equivalent of the CNI), so readers from elsewhere know where they stand.

Under 'Residency rules for overseas couples', lead with a one-line plain answer (the law sets no residency condition; the municipality may set its own) before the detail, so the heading's question is answered first.
